claims.text: Many-light direct illumination remains difficult in real time because only a small number of rays can be traced per pixel while important lights depend on visibility, material response, geometry, and emitter power.

evidence_excerpts: The algorithm first generates independent per-pixel candidates, tests the selected candidates for visibility, combines reservoirs from the previous frame, performs spatial reuse, and then shades the pixel.
claims.text: ReSTIR samples one-bounce direct lighting by repeatedly resampling light candidates and reusing useful samples across spatial neighbors and prior frames.

evidence_excerpts: Combining k reservoirs runs in O(k) time and is mathematically equivalent to reservoir sampling on the concatenated input streams.
claims.text: Reservoir sampling makes spatiotemporal reuse practical because a pixel can combine selected samples and weight sums from neighboring reservoirs without storing each candidate stream.

evidence_excerpts: The results section reports that the biased method has less variance but can show energy loss around shadow boundaries, sharp highlights, and complex geometry.
claims.text: The biased ReSTIR estimator lowers variance and improves visual quality at interactive render times, but it can lose energy and darken regions near geometric, visibility, or shading discontinuities.

evidence_excerpts: The analysis shows the traditional RIS weight underestimates the inverse PDF when some candidate PDFs are zero; MIS weights m(xz)=pz(xz)/sum_i pi(xz) restore an unbiased estimator.
claims.text: A modified RIS weight using candidate-PDF multiple importance weights can remove bias introduced by mixing samples from different pixel distributions, though visibility-aware unbiased reuse costs extra rays.

evidence_excerpts: The abstract reports equal-error 6x-60x faster for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x faster for the biased estimator, with up to 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles under 50 ms.
claims.text: ReSTIR achieves substantially faster equal-error rendering than the compared state-of-the-art many-light method, including reported 6x-60x speedups for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x for the biased estimator.

evidence_excerpts: Figure 2 states that denoisers cannot reconstruct missing features and that improved sampling quality lets existing denoisers produce better results.
claims.text: Improving the quality of direct-light samples before denoising can make existing denoisers more effective because denoisers cannot reconstruct image features absent from their input samples.

evidence_excerpts: The limitations section says reuse is less effective near disocclusions, lighting discontinuities, high geometric complexity, and fast moving lights, and that image buffers limit the method to the primary hit point.
claims.text: The method depends on useful spatial or temporal correlation and on image-space reservoirs, so performance degrades near disocclusions, fast lighting changes, high geometric complexity, and beyond first-hit direct lighting.

evidence_items.excerpt: Figure 1 reports a Zero Day frame with 11,000 dynamic emissive triangles rendered in 15 ms and an Amusement Park view with 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles rendered in 50 ms, both at 1920 x 1080 resolution.
evidence_items.overview: These timing and scene-size measurements anchor the paper's main practical claim: ReSTIR is not only a theoretical sampling method but a GPU implementation capable of real-time direct lighting in scenes with thousands to millions of dynamic emitters. The evidence is scene-specific and does not by itself establish performance for all hardware or content.
evidence_items.title: Dynamic Scene Timing Results

evidence_items.excerpt: The abstract reports that the unbiased estimator reaches equal error 6x-60x faster than state-of-the-art methods, while the biased estimator is 35x-65x faster but has some energy loss.
evidence_items.overview: This result directly supports the paper's performance claim and separates the unbiased and biased variants. The speedups are relative to the paper's comparison methods and error metric, so they should be read in the context of the tested scenes, GPU implementations, and direct-lighting task.
evidence_items.title: Equal-Error Speedup Claims

evidence_items.excerpt: The algorithm treats each reservoir's selected sample as a fresh sample with weight equal to the accumulated weight sum, producing a result equivalent to sampling over the combined input streams while requiring only reservoir state access.
evidence_items.overview: This formal algorithmic observation explains why ReSTIR can reuse candidates across pixels and frames without storing every candidate. It establishes the core mechanism behind the method's low memory footprint and effective candidate-count amplification.
evidence_items.title: Reservoir Combination Argument

evidence_items.excerpt: The derivation gives E[W(x,z) | xz=y] = 1/p(y) * |Z(y)|/M for mixed candidate PDFs, then replaces the uniform 1/M factor with weights m(xz) whose nonzero-PDF sum is one.
evidence_items.overview: This proof step identifies why naive reuse across different pixel distributions can be biased and how the estimator can be corrected. It is central to the distinction between ReSTIR's cheaper biased mode and its more expensive unbiased mode.
evidence_items.title: RIS Bias Correction Derivation

evidence_items.excerpt: Figure 11 compares RMAE over render time for MIS, Moreau et al.'s light BVH, streaming RIS, biased spatiotemporal reuse, unbiased spatiotemporal reuse, and biased spatial-only reuse; the text reports that biased spatiotemporal reuse has the lowest error at interactive render times.
evidence_items.overview: The error-curve comparison supports the claim that ReSTIR's reuse is useful beyond isolated image examples. It also clarifies the tradeoff: the biased version tends to win at interactive budgets, while bias can dominate at longer render times and the unbiased version can eventually become preferable.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Error Curve Results

evidence_items.excerpt: The limitations section states that image-buffer reservoirs make the method fast and memory efficient, but limit it to operations on the first camera-path vertex and make extension beyond first-hit direct lighting difficult.
evidence_items.overview: This limitation constrains how broadly the method can be applied. It distinguishes the demonstrated real-time primary-hit direct-lighting problem from harder global-illumination or deeper-path reuse settings that would require new data structures or clustering choices.
evidence_items.title: Image-Space Scope Limits

relations.rationale: Reservoir combination is the mechanism that makes ReSTIR's spatial and temporal light-candidate reuse practical.
The unbiased weighting analysis justifies reuse across reservoirs drawn from different pixel distributions.
The biased variant's lower variance explains why it produces strong interactive-time error reductions despite possible darkening.
Better input samples can improve downstream denoising and contribute to the reported quality advantage.
The limitations follow from the same image-space reservoir design that enables efficient reuse.

source.display_title: ReSTIR Makes Dynamic Direct Lighting Real-Time

source_date_inference.rationale: The ACM reference and page footer in the extracted source state publication date: July 2020.

sections.body: The source targets one-bounce direct lighting from many dynamic emissive surfaces under real-time ray budgets. It treats the problem as hard even for offline renderers because important lights depend jointly on visibility, BSDF response, geometry, and emitted power, while interactive applications cannot afford exhaustive shadow rays or heavy per-frame structures.
sections.heading: Problem Setting

sections.body: ReSTIR uses weighted reservoir sampling to keep a compact state per pixel: a selected light sample, accumulated weight information, and the number of candidates represented. Reservoirs can then be combined without recovering their original streams, letting spatial neighbors and previous frames contribute candidate information at low storage cost.
sections.heading: Reservoir Reuse Mechanism

sections.body: The paper is explicit that naive spatiotemporal reuse mixes different pixel distributions and can introduce bias. Its analysis shows how modified RIS weights and MIS-style balancing can preserve unbiasedness, but the practical unbiased path can require extra visibility tests. The biased path is cheaper and lower variance but may darken difficult boundaries.
sections.heading: Biased And Unbiased Modes

sections.body: The reported measurements connect the math to GPU rendering. The abstract gives equal-error speedups of 6x-60x for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x for the biased estimator, while figure captions report real-time images at 1920 x 1080 with 11,000 and 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles.
sections.heading: Performance Evidence

sections.body: ReSTIR is positioned as complementary to denoising rather than a replacement for it. The paper argues that denoisers cannot restore features missing from their input samples, so improving sample quality inside the renderer can make the denoiser's later reconstruction task better conditioned.
sections.heading: Denoising Interpretation

sections.body: The approach relies on spatial and temporal sample relevance. It is less effective around disocclusions, lighting discontinuities, fast moving lights, and high geometric complexity. Because the implementation stores reservoirs in image buffers, its demonstrated scope is primary-hit direct lighting rather than arbitrary deeper-path global illumination.
sections.heading: Assumptions And Limits

source_dossier.summary_long: This paper introduces ReSTIR, Reservoir-based Spatio-Temporal Importance Resampling, for real-time ray-traced direct lighting with many dynamic emitters. The core problem is that a renderer cannot trace shadow rays to all lights, and in real-time settings it may only afford a few rays per pixel. ReSTIR addresses that constraint by generating a small set of per-pixel light candidates, resampling them with a target distribution based on unshadowed path contribution, and storing only the selected sample, its weight, and the effective candidate count in a reservoir. The key algorithmic move is that reservoirs can be combined as if their original candidate streams had been concatenated, which lets nearby pixels and prior frames share useful sampling information without storing every candidate. This turns spatial and temporal coherence into better sampling PDFs inside the renderer rather than post-process filtering of colors. The paper also analyzes why naive reuse across pixels can introduce bias: neighboring pixels may have different target distributions, visibility, normals, and supports. It derives an unbiased correction using modified RIS weights and multiple-importance-style candidate-PDF weights, but notes that visibility-aware unbiased reuse can require additional shadow rays. As a result, the implementation offers both biased and unbiased variants. The biased version is faster and often lower variance at interactive budgets, but it can darken difficult regions such as shadow boundaries, highlights, or complex geometry. The reported results are substantial: the abstract claims equal-error speedups of 6x-60x for the unbiased estimator and 35x-65x for the biased estimator, and figures show scenes with 11,000 to 3.4 million dynamic emissive triangles rendered at 1920 x 1080 in tens of milliseconds. The method is strongest as a first-hit direct-lighting technique in scenes where neighboring pixels and previous frames provide relevant samples. It is weaker near disocclusions, fast moving lights, lighting discontinuities, and cases where image-space correlation breaks down; extending it beyond primary-hit direct lighting remains future work.
source_dossier.summary_short: ReSTIR treats real-time many-light direct illumination as a reservoir resampling problem. It stores compact per-pixel reservoirs, reuses selected candidates across neighbors and prior frames, and offers biased and unbiased modes. The result is fast GPU rendering with clear limits around discontinuities, weak correlation, and first-hit image-space scope.

summary: ReSTIR is a reservoir-based Monte Carlo method for real-time direct lighting from many dynamic emitters. It reuses light samples across pixels and frames, offers biased and unbiased variants, and reports large equal-error speedups on GPU scenes with thousands to millions of emissive triangles. Its main tradeoffs are bias and darkening in the cheaper mode, extra ray cost in the unbiased mode, and reduced benefit where image-space spatiotemporal correlation is weak.
